0.title: How We Got Our Bible: A Study in Divine Providence
0.essay:
The Bible you hold is a kind of miracle. Not only because its words are inspired, but because its survival — across three thousand years of copying, persecution, translation and printing — is itself the work of God. Kings burned it. Emperors banned it. Scribes made mistakes copying it. And yet here it is, unchanged in substance and undiminished in power, opened by millions every morning and found to be alive.

A study in the character of God

This is not mainly a course in ancient manuscripts or translation theory, though we will touch on both. It is a study of what kind of God we have. The God who spoke to Abraham, gave the law to Moses and breathed his words through Isaiah, Paul and John was not content to let those words disappear. He preserved them. He guided their copying, their collection into one book, their translation into the languages of the world and their arrival in your hands. The history of the Bible is, at every point, the history of a God who wants to be known.

The road ahead

We begin with the God who speaks — what it means that Scripture is breathed out by God. Then we ask how God’s people recognised which books belong in the Bible: first the Old Testament, then the New. We trace how the text was copied and preserved through the centuries, and how it was translated and given to the world, often at the cost of lives. We ask how to read it well. And finally we ask the question beneath all the others: why we can trust it.

Not just information

You can know all of this history and still open your Bible with cold eyes and a closed heart. The goal is not information about the Bible but meeting the God who gave it. Our hope is that by the end, every time you pick up your Bible you will feel its weight — not the weight of paper and ink, but the weight of what it is: the living word of the God who made you, redeemed you, and still speaks through these pages to make you like his Son.

1.title: The God Who Speaks
1.essay:
Every account of how we got the Bible has to begin here: with the God who speaks. The Bible is not a human book that happens to contain religious wisdom, nor a record of great saints’ spiritual experiences. It is God’s own self-disclosure in human words. Everything else depends on that.

Breathed out by God

“All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:16–17). The Greek word Paul uses, theopneustos, means “God-breathed”. This is its first known use in Greek literature; Paul may have coined it. He is not saying Scripture is inspiring in the way great art inspires us. He is saying it was exhaled by God — the direction is from God outward, not from human experience upward.

Notice the scope: “all Scripture” — not just the uplifting passages, but the genealogies, the laws and the laments too. And notice the purpose. Teaching shows us what to believe; reproof shows where we have gone wrong; correction shows how to get right; training in righteousness shows how to stay right. The result is completeness. The Bible is not one helpful resource among many for the Christian life; it is enough.

Carried along by the Spirit

Yet God’s breath came through real human authors. “Men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21). The word for “carried along” is used in Acts 27 of a ship driven by the wind. The sailors are still sailors; they use their skills and judgment. But the wind takes them where it wills. So Isaiah writes with Isaiah’s vocabulary, Paul argues with Paul’s logic, and Luke researches with a historian’s care (Luke 1:1–4) — and through all of it, the Spirit ensures that what they write is exactly what God intends to say.

This rules out two errors. The Bible is not mechanical dictation, as though the authors were passive typists. Nor is it merely human testimony from people with a strong sense of God. Theologians call the biblical view verbal plenary inspiration: verbal, because it extends to the words and not only the ideas; plenary, because it extends to all of Scripture. The Bible is fully human and fully divine — rather like the Lord it is about.

God’s final word

“Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:1–2). God spoke in pieces, through prophets, priests and kings, through promises and patterns. Then he spoke his final and fullest Word: his Son. The Old Testament is God speaking in preparation for Christ; the New Testament is God speaking in explanation of Christ. Every page is, in some sense, about him.

A word that does things

God treats his word not just as a message but as an agent he sends. “As the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there but water the earth… so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose” (Isaiah 55:10–11). Wherever it is faithfully read or preached, it is at work, often invisibly. That is the comfort behind every sermon that seems to fall flat and every conversation about Christ that seems to go nowhere.

And because Scripture is God-breathed, it carries God’s authority. To believe it is to believe God; to disobey it is to disobey him. That is why the Reformers insisted on sola Scriptura: God’s word stands over every tradition, council, theological system and personal experience.

Inspiration and illumination

Inspiration was a completed work: the Spirit breathed out Scripture through the biblical authors, and that work is done. Illumination continues: the same Spirit opens readers’ minds and hearts to understand and receive what has already been given. When you read Ephesians today you are not receiving new revelation, but the Spirit’s light on revelation already given.

The Bereans showed the right instinct. When Paul preached, “they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so” (Acts 17:11), and Luke calls them noble for it. Scripture sits in judgment over preaching, not the other way round. In an age when “God told me…” can carry more weight than what the Bible actually says, it is worth remembering: God has spoken, fully and sufficiently, in the sixty-six books he breathed out. The longing for something more is often not spiritual sensitivity but dissatisfaction with what he has already given — and what he has given is enough.

For reflection

What difference does it make that Scripture is “breathed out” rather than merely “inspiring”? How does the picture of a ship carried by the wind help you hold together the human and divine sides of the Bible? Where are you tempted to treat your own experience as more authoritative than Scripture?

2.title: The Old Testament Canon: How Israel Knew
2.essay:
How do we know which books belong in the Old Testament? Not because a committee once voted on them, but because God’s people recognised his voice in them — and because Jesus himself put his seal on the Scriptures Israel had received.

What “canon” means

The word comes from the Greek kanōn, a measuring rod. The canon is the list of books that “measure up” — that carry God’s authority. For the Old Testament, the question was largely settled by the time of Jesus. The Hebrew Bible contained the same thirty-nine books as the Protestant Old Testament, though Jews counted them as twenty-four by combining some (Samuel, Kings and the twelve minor prophets, for example) and arranged them in three parts: the Law (Torah), the Prophets (Nevi’im) and the Writings (Ketuvim).

Jesus’ Bible

Jesus spoke of “everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms” (Luke 24:44) — naming the three parts of the Hebrew Bible, with the Psalms heading the Writings. He debated from these Scriptures, quoted them when tempted, read them in the synagogue and declared that they were all about him. Another saying confirms their scope. He spoke of the blood of the righteous shed “from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah” (Matthew 23:35). Abel is in Genesis, the first book of the Hebrew Bible; Zechariah’s murder is in 2 Chronicles, the last book in its traditional order. It is as if we said “from Genesis to Revelation”. The canon Jesus endorsed is the canon we carry.

How Israel recognised God’s word

From the beginning, God’s written word was set apart. Moses wrote the law in a book and had it placed beside the ark of the covenant (Deuteronomy 31:24–26), the symbol of God’s presence. After the exile, Ezra read the Book of the Law to the assembled people from early morning until midday, the Levites explained it, and the people wept and then celebrated (Nehemiah 8). Scripture was already functioning as the fixed standard by which God’s people lived.

The marks of these books were recognised rather than imposed: they came from a recognised prophet or someone closely associated with one; they agreed with the law already given; and they carried the unmistakable ring of “Thus says the LORD”. The Reformers, following Calvin, spoke of Scripture as self-authenticating: the church does not give Scripture its authority but recognises the authority it already has, and the Holy Spirit himself persuades believers that it is God’s word (Westminster Confession 1.5). As one writer has put it, the canon is not the church’s gift to the word, but the word’s gift to the church.

A gathering of rabbis at Yavneh (Jamnia) around AD 90 is sometimes said to have “decided” the canon. In fact there was probably no formal council at all. The rabbis discussed whether books such as Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs fitted with the rest — border questions that show the canon was already established.

What about the Apocrypha?

Roman Catholic and Orthodox Bibles contain extra books — among them Tobit, Judith, 1 and 2 Maccabees, Sirach and the Wisdom of Solomon, with additions to Daniel and Esther. They were written roughly between 200 BC and AD 100, preserved in the Greek Septuagint and read by many Jews and early Christians. But they were not part of the Hebrew Scriptures Jesus endorsed. The New Testament quotes the Old Testament hundreds of times but never cites these books as Scripture. The Jewish writers Philo and Josephus did not count them. Even Jerome, translator of the Latin Vulgate, said they could be read for edification but not to establish doctrine. Some contain historical errors, and 2 Maccabees 12 is used to support prayers for the dead. The Council of Trent made them binding for Roman Catholics only in 1546, in response to the Reformation. They can be read with profit as history and devotion, but they do not carry the authority of God-breathed Scripture.

Why it matters

When King Josiah’s servants found the Book of the Law in the neglected temple, Josiah tore his clothes and wept (2 Kings 22). He recognised at once the voice of God and how far his people had strayed. The reformation that followed came not from new revelation but from the rediscovery of what God had already given.

Canonical boundaries are not a matter of church politics. If you add 2 Maccabees, you gain a basis for praying for the dead; if you add later “gospels”, you get a different Jesus. Knowing why the thirty-nine books belong gives confidence every time you open the Old Testament: this is the body of writing Jesus himself called the word of God.

For reflection

How does Jesus’ use of the Old Testament settle its contents? What is the difference between the church creating the canon and recognising it? Why does it matter whether books such as 2 Maccabees are counted as Scripture?

3.title: The New Testament Canon: The Church Recognises What God Breathed
3.essay:
The New Testament did not fall from heaven as a bound volume. It emerged through the life of the early church over its first few centuries. But it was never the church’s invention. The twenty-seven books were recognised as Scripture because they were already working as God’s word in the churches that received them.

Recognised by the apostles themselves

The awareness of new Scripture began within the New Testament itself. Peter, writing near the end of his life, places Paul’s letters alongside “the other Scriptures” (2 Peter 3:15–16), using the word the New Testament reserves for Holy Scripture. Paul introduces two quotations with “the Scripture says”: one from Deuteronomy, and the other — “The laborer deserves his wages” (1 Timothy 5:18) — words found in Luke 10:7. Within a generation of Jesus, his words as recorded in the Gospels were being treated on a level with the law of Moses.

Behind this lies Jesus’ promise to the apostles: “the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you” (John 14:26). The Gospels and letters are not the apostles’ best recollections, gradually edited; they are the Spirit keeping that promise.

Three marks of a New Testament book

As the church received and read these writings, three questions guided it. Apostolic: did the book come from an apostle or someone closely associated with one — Mark with Peter, Luke with Paul, James and Jude as brothers of the Lord? Catholic: was it received and used by the churches everywhere, not just in one place? Genuine apostolic writings spread; forgeries tended to be local and late. Orthodox: did it agree with the apostolic faith already received? A book that contradicted the gospel could not be apostolic, whatever name it claimed.

Marcion and the “lost gospels”

Around AD 144 a wealthy shipowner named Marcion arrived in Rome with a slimmed-down Bible: an edited version of Luke and ten of Paul’s letters, cleansed of everything that connected Jesus with the God of the Old Testament. The church rejected him — and in doing so made clear what it already held: all four Gospels, the Old Testament as the foundation of the New, and the wider apostolic writings. Irenaeus and Tertullian appealed to these as the church’s inheritance. Marcion did not create the canon; he revealed that it already existed. A list from about AD 170, the Muratorian Fragment, already names a collection remarkably close to ours.

The so-called “lost gospels” — of Thomas, Philip, Judas — were never lost. They were examined and rejected. They were written in the second and third centuries, after the apostles had died; they present a Gnostic Jesus who teaches secret knowledge, quite unlike the Jesus of Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; and the churches did not use them. Valuable early Christian writings such as the Didache, 1 Clement and the Shepherd of Hermas were read with respect, but recognised as coming after the apostles.

By the fourth century the historian Eusebius could describe books as universally acknowledged, disputed or rejected — and the acknowledged books, together with those disputed but widely used (James, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude), make up our twenty-seven. When the Council of Carthage listed them in 397, it was confirming what the churches had long practised, not imposing something new.

A closed canon

The New Testament ends with a solemn warning not to add to or take away from the words of Revelation (Revelation 22:18–19). Though it applies directly to that book, it fits the whole canon: God’s revelation in his Son is complete. The Spirit still illumines and applies Scripture, but he does not produce new Scripture. We wait not for new revelation, but for the full unfolding of what has been revealed.

Every generation’s Marcion

Every age has its Marcion — someone offering a simpler, more appealing Jesus built by selection. In the 1980s and 1990s the Jesus Seminar voted on the authenticity of Jesus’ sayings with coloured beads and arrived at a Jesus who never spoke of judgment. Popular novels have claimed that power-hungry councils suppressed the real Jesus. The answer is the same as the early church’s: we have the apostolic witness — four Gospels written within living memory of Jesus, and letters of Paul written earlier still, resting on eyewitness testimony. The canon is not the product of church politics. It is the preserved voice of those who walked with the risen Lord.

For reflection

What do 2 Peter 3:16 and 1 Timothy 5:18 show about how early the New Testament was recognised as Scripture? Why did the church reject Marcion and the Gnostic gospels? How would you answer someone who says the Bible was chosen by a council for political reasons?

4.title: Copying God’s Word: Providence in Parchment and Ink
4.essay:
Once God had breathed out his word, a new question arose: how would it survive the centuries — the collapse of empires, the burning of libraries, the slow errors of hand-copying? The answer is one of the most remarkable stories in history, and it is a story of preservation, not corruption.

The care of the scribes

Jewish scribes copied the Hebrew Scriptures with astonishing devotion. The Masoretes, who worked roughly from AD 500 to 1000, counted the letters of every book and knew the middle letter of the Torah. They checked letters per column and per page. A scroll with too many errors was retired from worship and reverently buried. Their work produced the Masoretic Text, the standard Hebrew Old Testament for a thousand years.

A stone thrown into a cave

In 1947 a Bedouin shepherd threw a stone into a cave above the Dead Sea and heard pottery break. Inside were jars containing ancient scrolls — among them a complete scroll of Isaiah, copied around 125 BC, a thousand years older than any Hebrew manuscript previously known. When scholars compared it with the Masoretic Text, they found it essentially the same in substance. A thousand years of copying by hand, by candlelight, across generations — and the text had been preserved with extraordinary faithfulness. The Dead Sea Scrolls are not a threat to the Old Testament; they are a monument to its preservation.

The best-attested book of the ancient world

The New Testament survives in more than 5,800 Greek manuscripts, from tiny papyrus fragments to complete books. One fragment of John’s Gospel, known as P52, is dated by many scholars to the first half of the second century; Codex Sinaiticus, from the fourth century, contains the whole New Testament. Most classical authors survive in a few dozen or a few hundred copies, usually made many centuries after they wrote — yet no one doubts what Caesar or Plato wrote. By any standard of ancient history, the New Testament is overwhelmingly attested.

Copyists did make mistakes: spelling differences, words in a different order, a line accidentally repeated. Textual criticism is the careful work of comparing manuscripts to recover the original wording, and it is possible precisely because we have so many. Some popular books, such as Bart Ehrman’s Misquoting Jesus (2005), present these variations as a reason for doubt. But the vast majority are trivial, and no doctrine of the Christian faith rests on a disputed reading. The abundance of manuscripts is a blessing, not a liability.

The Old Testament is a little more complex. It came down in two main streams — the Hebrew Masoretic Text and the Greek Septuagint — and the Dead Sea Scrolls show that both are ancient. The apostles often quoted the Septuagint, which is why some Old Testament quotations in the New Testament read slightly differently from our English Old Testaments, translated from the Hebrew.

The God who keeps his word

Behind the scribes stands the faithfulness of God. “The words of the LORD are pure words, like silver refined in a furnace on the ground, purified seven times” (Psalm 12:6). Jesus trusted the Scriptures he held: “until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished” (Matthew 5:18). “The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever” (Isaiah 40:8). Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome have withered; the word stands.

Reformed theology speaks of providential preservation. It does not claim that every manuscript is perfect, or that copying was miraculous in the way inspiration was. It says that God, by his “singular care and providence”, has kept his word pure in all ages (Westminster Confession 1.8), so that we can know with confidence what he said. When Paul says the Old Testament “was written for our instruction” (Romans 15:4), he assumes the text in his hands is the text God gave. Every discovery since has confirmed that assumption.

Opening your Bible with confidence

Ezra carried the Torah back to Jerusalem after the exile, having “set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel” (Ezra 7:10). The word had survived the catastrophe that destroyed the temple. When you hear that the Bible has been changed beyond recognition, remember the scribe counting his letters, the monk in his scriptorium and the shepherd throwing stones into a cave — all unknowing servants of a God who does not let his word fail.

For reflection

What do the Dead Sea Scrolls show about the copying of the Old Testament? Why is the number of New Testament manuscripts an encouragement rather than a problem? How does God’s faithfulness to his word strengthen your trust in him?

5.title: Giving the Bible to the World: Translation as Providence
5.essay:
God breathed out his word in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek. But he never meant it to stay there. From the beginning there has been a God-given drive to put Scripture into the languages of ordinary people — a story of courage, opposition, sacrifice and grace.

Pentecost: the gospel in every tongue

The pattern was set at Pentecost. When the Spirit came, Jews from many nations were bewildered, “because each one was hearing them speak in his own language” (Acts 2:6). The gospel was not tied to one sacred language. Babel’s confusion began to be undone, and the church learned that the good news must always be translated. Heaven’s song confirms the goal: Christ “ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9). Paul’s chain of reasoning — “how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard?” (Romans 10:14) — requires that the word cross every language barrier.

Greek and Latin

The first great translation was the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament made in Alexandria from around 280 BC. A legend said seventy-two scholars produced it; whatever the details, it put the Hebrew Scriptures into the common language of the Mediterranean world just in time for the New Testament to be written in that same language. The apostles often quote it.

Later, Jerome’s Latin Vulgate (382–405) gave the western church the whole Bible in its common tongue. For a thousand years monks copied it by hand, preserving both the text and much of European civilisation with it.

Wycliffe and Tyndale

The drama of the English Bible begins with John Wycliffe, whose circle produced the first complete English Bible around 1380, copied by hand from the Latin. Wycliffe believed every English ploughman should be able to read Scripture. Church authorities were furious. He died in his bed, but in 1428, on the order of the Council of Constance, his bones were dug up and burned. His Bible survived.

William Tyndale went further. Working from the Hebrew and Greek, he produced the first printed English New Testament in 1526. He spent years as a fugitive in Germany and the Low Countries, translating in secret, until a friend betrayed him. After sixteen months in prison he was strangled and burned at Vilvoorde, near Brussels, in 1536. His last words are recorded as, “Lord, open the King of England’s eyes.” Within three years Henry VIII had authorised the Great Bible, built largely on Tyndale’s work. Much of the King James Version’s language is Tyndale’s.

The King James Version

Commissioned after the Hampton Court Conference of 1604, the King James Version (1611) was the work of forty-seven scholars in six companies. They used the best Hebrew and Greek texts available to them and drew heavily on Tyndale and earlier English Bibles. The result shaped English prayer, preaching and literature for four centuries. Its translators did not regard it as final; their preface defends the value of revision. But it remains one of the great gifts of God’s providence to the English-speaking world.

Choosing a translation today

Modern translations sit on a spectrum. Formal translations such as the ESV and NASB render the original word for word as far as English allows — ideal for study. Functional translations such as the NIV and NLT render the thought in natural modern English — excellent for reading and for newcomers. Paraphrases such as The Message retell the text freely; they can freshen a familiar passage but are not suitable for careful study. No translation is perfect, but every faithful translation is an instrument of the God who breathed out the original.

The unfinished task

According to the Wycliffe Global Alliance, by 2024 the whole Bible existed in over 750 languages, the New Testament in about 1,700 more, and some portion of Scripture in well over three thousand. Yet many hundreds of languages still have nothing. Zephaniah foresaw a day when God would give the peoples “pure speech, that all of them may call upon the name of the LORD” (Zephaniah 3:9). Every translation project moves toward that day.

We receive our Bibles almost without noticing — dozens of translations, free on our phones. But the Bible in your hand was bought at a price: Wycliffe’s followers burned for distributing hand-copied pages, Tyndale strangled at the stake, refugees in Geneva labouring over the Geneva Bible, and today thousands of translators working in remote places. Read it accordingly.

For reflection

How does Pentecost shape the church’s commitment to translation? What do Wycliffe and Tyndale teach you about the value of the Bible in your own language? How might you support the work of translation for peoples who still have no Scripture?

6.title: How to Read It Well: Profiting from the Bible God Preserved
6.essay:
All this history — inspiration, canon, scribes, translators — arrives at one moment: you, with a Bible in your hands. The God who breathed it out and preserved it through the centuries means to use it to make you complete, equipped for every good work, like his Son. The question is whether you will come to it in a way that lets him.

Tools, not Scripture

A few practical things first. The chapter divisions in our Bibles were added by Stephen Langton, later Archbishop of Canterbury, in the early thirteenth century; the New Testament verse numbers by the French printer Robert Estienne in 1551. They are useful for finding our place, but they are not inspired, and they can encourage us to read verses as detachable sayings. Romans 8:28 is a glorious promise, but it means something specific in the flow of verses 18–30. Read passages, not just verses.

Use a faithful translation you will actually read. A formal translation such as the ESV or NASB rewards slow study; the NIV is excellent for reading large sections; a paraphrase can occasionally open a familiar text with fresh eyes. Most of all, read one consistently enough to know it.

Pray before you read

“Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). The psalmist does not sit down confident in his own ability. He knows the text is full of wonders he cannot see without help, and he asks for it. The Puritans spoke of coming to Scripture with a prepared heart: praying first, reading with expectation that God will speak, and slowing down when something arrests you rather than pressing on to finish the chapter. The Bible is not a newspaper to be processed. It is a conversation with a person.

Meditate, delight and do

God told Joshua, “This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night” (Joshua 1:8). The Hebrew word for meditate suggests murmuring a text aloud, chewing on it. Take a verse or phrase with you into the day and turn it over: what does it mean, promise, demand?

The first psalm describes the blessed person whose “delight is in the law of the LORD”: “He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season” (Psalm 1:2–3). The secret is not crisis-reading when trouble comes, but daily, delighted feeding — a tree drawing continually from the stream.

And reading must lead to doing. James warns of the man who looks into a mirror and goes away forgetting what he saw. “But the one who looks into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and perseveres, being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, he will be blessed in his doing” (James 1:25). Bible reading that never moves toward obedience is, James says, self-deception.

A living word

“For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12). It reaches places no friend or counsellor can reach. That is why Reformed Christians call Scripture a means of grace: the Spirit uses it to convict, comfort, strengthen and change. The Second Helvetic Confession could even say, “The preaching of the Word of God is the Word of God.”

Two kinds of reading belong together. Reading large portions — perhaps through the whole Bible in a year — keeps the big story alive and lets Scripture sweep over you. Studying a passage slowly, perhaps with a good commentary, keeps us honest about what it actually says. The devotional reader needs the student’s care; the student needs the devotional heart.

Feeding your soul

George Müller, who ran orphanages in Bristol by faith and prayer, discovered in his thirties that he had been reading the Bible mainly to prepare for ministry. He changed his practice: each morning he read Scripture to feed his own soul. “I saw more clearly than ever,” he wrote, “that the first great and primary business to which I ought to attend every day was to have my soul happy in the Lord.” Decades of extraordinary faith flowed from that daily feeding.

The danger of having the Bible on our phones in thirty seconds is casual familiarity — the word as background noise. The remedy is simple, ancient and demanding: open it daily, prayerfully, expectantly, intending to do what it says. The God who preserved it for you has not finished speaking through it.

For reflection

What helps you come to the Bible with a prepared heart? Which verse could you carry with you and meditate on this week? Where has your reading stopped short of doing what God says?

7.title: Why We Can Trust It
7.essay:
The Bible makes extraordinary claims: about God, human sin, the identity of Jesus, judgment and eternal life. Claims like these demand that we ask whether the book making them can be trusted. The answer comes from several directions at once — and they point the same way.

Always ready to give a reason

Peter tells believers, “in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15). The word for “defense” is apologia, used of a case made in court. Our hope should be something we can explain, not merely feel. But the defence flows from hearts that honour Christ, and it is made with gentleness, not contempt.

History and archaeology

Luke begins his Gospel like a historian, having “followed all things closely for some time past”, so that Theophilus “may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught” (Luke 1:3–4). His care has been repeatedly confirmed. Titles of officials in Acts once thought mistaken — such as the “politarchs” of Thessalonica — have turned up on inscriptions.

Archaeology has confirmed much else. The pool of Bethesda (John 5:2), once dismissed as a theological invention, was excavated in Jerusalem. An inscription found at Caesarea in 1961 bears the name of Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judea. The Moabite Stone (discovered 1868) describes King Mesha of Moab, known from 2 Kings 3. The Tel Dan inscription (1993) mentions the “house of David”, the first reference to David outside the Bible. Hezekiah’s tunnel and the Cyrus Cylinder, recording Cyrus’s policy of returning exiled peoples (compare Ezra 1), add to a growing case. The Bible is rooted in the real world it describes.

Prophecy fulfilled

God himself points to prophecy as evidence: “I am God, and there is none like me, declaring the end from the beginning” (Isaiah 46:9–10). Isaiah 53 was written centuries before Jesus — the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, copied around 125 BC, puts that beyond doubt. Yet it describes a servant “pierced for our transgressions”, “crushed for our iniquities”, who makes “his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death” and afterwards sees his offspring (Isaiah 53:5, 9–10). The New Testament points to many more fulfilments: birth in Bethlehem (Micah 5:2), the king riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9), thirty pieces of silver (Zechariah 11:12–13), garments divided by lot (Psalm 22:18), no bone broken (Psalm 34:20). Coincidence is a hard explanation to sustain.

One story, many authors

Some forty authors wrote over about fifteen hundred years, in three languages, on three continents. Yet the result is not a jumble but one story — creation, fall, redemption, new creation — with Christ at its centre. The promise to Abraham is fulfilled in Christ (Galatians 3:16); the Passover lamb is explained by the Lamb of God (John 1:29); the temple gives way to the true temple, his body (John 2:21); the Day of Atonement is fulfilled in his once-for-all sacrifice (Hebrews 9–10). That is not the consistency of careful editing, but of one divine Author guiding the whole.

The resurrection

At the heart of it all is the resurrection. In 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 Paul hands on a summary he had “received” — very likely in Jerusalem when he met Peter and James a few years after the crucifixion (Galatians 1:18–19). It names witnesses: Peter, the Twelve, James, and more than five hundred at once, most of them still alive when Paul wrote — in effect, an invitation to go and ask them. In Jerusalem even Jesus’ opponents did not deny the empty tomb; they tried to explain it away (Matthew 28:11–15). The best explanation of the evidence remains the one the disciples gave from the start: he is risen.

The witness of the Spirit

Yet the deepest reason ordinary Christians across the centuries have trusted their Bibles is not scholarship. Calvin taught what he called the inner witness of the Holy Spirit: “the same Spirit, therefore, who has spoken through the mouths of the prophets must penetrate into our hearts to persuade us that they faithfully proclaimed what had been divinely commanded” (Institutes 1.7.4). The evidences are real and persuasive; they show the Bible is credible. But the Spirit produces conviction. He does not ask us to believe against the evidence, but opens our eyes to see what the evidence points to.

When the Ethiopian official read Isaiah 53 on a desert road, the evidence was in his hands, and the Spirit was in Philip’s words. Philip “told him the good news about Jesus” (Acts 8:35), and he was baptised at the first water they came to. That is how trust in Scripture is born. So give the sceptic your reasons — and then pray, because only the Spirit can show that what all the evidence points to is not merely a reliable book, but the living word of a loving God.

For reflection

Which strand of evidence for the Bible’s trustworthiness do you find most helpful? How would you explain the resurrection evidence to a friend? Why do both the evidence and the Spirit’s witness matter?
